What the differences mean

  • Running cost: Brio 520 and Moderna 720: 0.76 kWh × 365 = 277 kWh × 18.16¢ = about $50 a year. Brio 430: 0.79 × 365 × 18.16¢ = about $52. Brio 130: 0.60 × 365 × 18.16¢ = about $40. These are standby figures, so a cooler you draw water from will cost somewhat more.
  • Five-year cost: Brio 520: $329.99 + 5 × $50.38 = about $582. Brio 430: $174.99 + 5 × $52.36 = about $437.
  • Cold glasses per hour: Brio 520: 0.74 gal × 128 oz ÷ 6 = about 15.8 six-oz cups at 42°F. Brio 430: 0.53 × 128 ÷ 6 = about 11.3 cups at 47°F. Avalon A4: 2.5 L = 84.5 oz ÷ 6 = about 14 cups at ≤47°F (Avalon's own rating, not a lab test).
  • Hot water per hour: Brio 520: 46 × 6 oz = 276 oz, about 2.2 gal at 167°F. Brio 130: 8 × 6 oz = 48 oz, though at 196°F.
  • Moderna premium: $449.99 − $329.99 = $120 more than the 520, with identical test figures.

What ENERGY STAR's test record shows, and which coolers aren't on it

The EPA's certified water-cooler list was last updated on 2026-11-08. It records three things for each listed model: the energy needed to keep water hot and cold for 24 hours with nothing drawn, how much cold water the cooler delivers per hour, and how much hot water. It also records the temperature each was measured at. The Brio 520 is listed under one record with the Moderna 720 and 730 and the Brio 420. They share one result: 0.76 kWh/day, 0.74 gal/h cold at 42°F and 46 cups/h hot at 167°F. Primo's 601202 bottom-load family has exactly the same five figures.

Avalon has no model on the list. A full-text search for Avalon returns no records. Target's A4 listing says 'Energy Star Certified', but on the same page an answer from Avalon's brand expert says 'No it is not'. Bob Vila also lists the A4 as certified. The A4 figures in the table come from Avalon's manual: 2.5 L/h cold at ≤47°F and 4 L/h hot at ≥185°F. Those are the maker's ratings, measured differently from the EPA test, so treat them as approximate when comparing.

Temperatures differ too. The 520 was tested 5°F colder than the 430 and 740 (42°F against 47°F). Brio's 130 is a Low Capacity cooler: it was tested at 196°F hot but delivers only 8 cups of hot water an hour.

Not recommended

The Brio 740 is Brio's most expensive plain bottom-loader at $649.99. In the EPA test it delivered only 0.08 gal of cold water an hour: 0.08 × 128 ÷ 6 = about 1.7 six-oz cups, at 47°F. That is about a ninth of the 520's output for nearly twice the price. Its lower standby energy reflects its Low Capacity class, not better efficiency.
